explanation: A fund that trades on an exchange like a stock, holding a basket of assets (e.g. all the companies in an index). Lets you buy diversified exposure in a single trade.
Price-to-Earnings ratio: a stock's share price divided by its earnings per share. A quick gauge of how expensive a stock is relative to the profit it generates.
The Federal Reserve, the US central bank. It sets interest rates and controls the money supply, which ripples through nearly every asset class worldwide.
A company's total value on the stock market: share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. Used to compare company size.
A portion of a company's profit paid out to shareholders, usually quarterly. Not all companies pay one — many reinvest profits into growth instead.
A loan you make to a government or company. They pay you regular interest (the coupon) and return your principal when the bond matures.
The fixed interest rate a bond pays its holder, expressed as a percentage of the bond's face value, usually paid annually or semi-annually.
The income return on an investment, usually expressed as a percentage of its price. A bond's yield moves opposite to its price.
Spreading investments across different assets so a loss in one doesn't sink the whole portfolio. The classic 'don't put all your eggs in one basket.'
How much and how fast an asset's price swings up and down. Higher volatility means bigger potential gains and losses.
A sustained period of rising prices, typically 20%+ off a low, paired with investor optimism.
A sustained period of falling prices, typically a 20%+ drop from a recent high, paired with pessimism.
How quickly and easily an asset can be converted to cash without significantly affecting its price. Stocks are highly liquid; real estate is not.
How you split your money across asset classes — stocks, bonds, cash, real estate, etc. — based on your goals and risk tolerance.
A fund designed to track a market index (like the S&P 500) rather than trying to beat it. Low-cost and hands-off by design.
Shares of large, well-established, financially sound companies with a long track record of reliable performance.
Initial Public Offering: the first time a private company sells shares to the public, becoming a publicly traded company.
An order to buy or sell a security immediately at the best available current price.
An order to buy or sell a security only at a specific price or better. Gives you price control but no guarantee it'll execute.
Periodically buying or selling assets to bring your portfolio back to its target allocation as markets drift it out of line.
The profit made when you sell an asset for more than you paid for it. Taxed differently depending on how long you held it.
The rate at which prices rise over time, eroding the purchasing power of cash. A key reason people invest rather than just save.
The cost of borrowing money, or the return on lending it, expressed as a percentage. Central bank rate changes move nearly every market.
Interest earned on both your original investment and on the interest it's already accumulated. The engine behind long-term wealth growth.
The annual fee a fund charges investors, expressed as a percentage of assets invested. Lower is generally better for long-term returns.
A short-term drop of 10% or more in a market index from its recent peak — smaller and usually less severe than a bear market.
A significant decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months, commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of falling GDP.
Gross Domestic Product: the total value of all goods and services produced in a country. The headline measure of economic health.
A company increases its share count (e.g. 2-for-1) while proportionally lowering the price per share. Total value held is unchanged.
A firm that continuously quotes buy and sell prices for a security, providing liquidity so trades can happen quickly.
Borrowing shares to sell now, betting the price falls so you can buy them back cheaper later and pocket the difference. High risk — losses are theoretically unlimited.
Borrowing money from a broker to buy more securities than your cash alone would allow. Amplifies both gains and losses.
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price, which smooths out the impact of volatility over time.
A broad category of investments with similar characteristics — stocks, bonds, cash, real estate, commodities, crypto.
A line plotting interest rates across different bond maturities. When it 'inverts' (short-term rates exceed long-term), it's historically flagged as a recession warning.
The overall attitude of investors toward a market or asset — optimistic (bullish) or pessimistic (bearish) — which can move prices independent of fundamentals.
State-level regulations in the US requiring securities offerings to be registered, protecting investors from fraud.
A cryptocurrency designed to hold a steady value, usually pegged 1:1 to a currency like the US dollar.
The recurring pattern of expansion and contraction markets move through over time — growth, peak, decline, trough, repeat.
The increase in a property's value over time, driven by factors like location, demand, and improvements.
Capitalization rate: a property's annual net income divided by its purchase price, used to estimate a real estate investment's potential return.
Real Estate Investment Trust: a company that owns income-producing real estate, letting investors gain property exposure without buying physical buildings.
The total value of everything you own (assets) minus everything you owe (liabilities). The single-number snapshot of financial position.
The original purchase price of an investment, used to calculate capital gains or losses when you sell it.
An investment's full gain or loss, combining price appreciation with any income received (dividends, interest, rent).
How much investment loss you're personally willing and able to withstand, which should shape your asset allocation.
A bond issued by a highly creditworthy, financially stable government or corporation — considered low default risk.
A grade (like AAA or BB) assigned to a bond issuer reflecting its ability to repay debt. Lower ratings mean higher risk and typically higher yields.
The date a bond's principal is due to be repaid in full to the bondholder.
Often called the 'fear index' — it measures expected stock market volatility over the next 30 days based on S&P 500 options pricing.
A strategy of buying and holding broad, low-cost investments (like index funds) rather than actively picking stocks or timing the market.
A strategy where a manager or investor actively picks securities, aiming to outperform the broader market — usually at higher cost and risk.
A decentralized, tamper-resistant digital ledger that records transactions across many computers — the underlying technology behind cryptocurrencies.
The risk that you won't be able to sell an asset quickly without accepting a lower price, because there aren't enough buyers at the moment.
A statistical measure of how much an investment's returns swing away from their average. Higher standard deviation means more volatile, less predictable returns.
The average of squared deviations from the mean return — the math behind standard deviation (which is just its square root), used to quantify how spread out returns are.
A measure of how much an asset moves relative to the overall market. A beta of 1 tracks the market; above 1 amplifies market swings, below 1 dampens them.
The excess return an investment generates above what its risk (beta) would predict. Positive alpha means it beat expectations; it's the number active managers chase.
Return earned per unit of risk taken: (return minus risk-free rate) divided by standard deviation. Lets you compare investments with different volatility on equal footing.
Like the Sharpe ratio, but only penalizes downside volatility — since investors don't actually mind upside swings, just downside risk.
A measure from -1 to +1 of how closely two assets move together. Near 0 or negative correlation is what makes diversification actually reduce risk.
A statistic from 0 to 100% showing how much of a fund's movement is explained by its benchmark index. High R-squared means it closely tracks the index; low means it doesn't.
Compound Annual Growth Rate: the smoothed annual return an investment would need to grow from its starting to ending value, ignoring the bumpy path in between.
The average price of an asset over a set recent period (e.g. 50 or 200 days), recalculated daily. Smooths out day-to-day noise to reveal the underlying trend.
A statistical method for measuring the relationship between a security's returns and one or more factors (like the market), used to estimate beta and alpha.
An estimate of the maximum expected loss on a portfolio over a set time period, at a given confidence level (e.g. 95%) — a common way to size downside risk.
The largest peak-to-trough decline an investment has experienced, expressed as a percentage. A key measure of how bad the worst-case ride has actually been.
A measure of how lopsided a return distribution is. Positive skew means occasional large gains; negative skew means occasional large losses — both hide behind the same average return.

A measure of how likely extreme outcomes are compared to a normal distribution. High kurtosis ('fat tails') means bigger surprises — good and bad — happen more often than a simple average would suggest.
A modeling technique that runs thousands of randomized scenarios to estimate the range of possible outcomes for a portfolio, rather than relying on a single projected average.
The set of portfolios that offer the highest expected return for each level of risk. Portfolios below the frontier are considered suboptimal — you could get more return for the same risk.
